Severity

Medium — Configured JA4 Block Connection or Domain can leave the triggering approved-destination tunnel active, and all block scopes can forward buffered bytes before the decision. Exploitation needs listener access, an allowlisted hostname with usable binding, 16 seeded distinct fingerprints for that ordinal, and a 17th valid SNI-matching ClientHello. The approved destination restriction remains, and deployment impact is unknown.

Severity rises if the approved endpoint exposes high-value capabilities and JA4 block is relied on for containment; it falls if only Notify or Ignore is configured or the listener is unreachable.

Impact assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: The security tripwire fails to terminate the anomalous flow, but the destination remains restricted to the approved endpoint.

Likelihood assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: After baseline saturation, the control-flow bypass is deterministic; setup and configuration prerequisites narrow exposure.

Remediation

Evaluate and record JA4 overflow immediately after ClientHello validation, before flushing the Hello or any buffered trailing bytes. Apply the configured action before upstream I/O and retain the change signal if a subsequent write fails. Close the triggering slot for Block Connection and Block Domain; for Domain also close siblings and latch future matching flows, and for All close all slots. Make the caller stop processing a closed slot.

Tests:

  • Configure JA4 Block Connection; saturate one ordinal's baseline and verify the triggering slot closes before any upstream write.
  • Repeat with JA4 Block Domain and verify the triggering slot, sibling flows, and future flows are blocked.
  • Confirm Notify and All actions retain their intended behavior.
  • With ja4 = { action = "block", scope = "connection" }, fill the baseline and verify the 17th distinct ClientHello closes its own tunnel before bytes reach upstream.
  • With scope = "fqdn", verify the triggering and sibling tunnels close and later CONNECT requests for that ordinal are refused.
  • With scope = "all", verify no pending client bytes are sent after the block decision.
  • Seed 16 distinct accepted JA4s, configure Block All, send a 17th fingerprint with pipelined application bytes, and assert no bytes reach upstream before the block.
  • Force an upstream write failure and assert the JA4 change signal is still retained.
  • Seed 16 distinct JA4 fingerprints, trigger a 17th under Block Connection, and assert the current tunnel closes before relay.
  • Repeat under Block Domain and assert both the triggering and other current matching tunnels close, while future matching CONNECT requests are refused.
  • Verify Block All and notify/ignore behavior remain correct.
  • After seeding 16 distinct JA4s, assert a 17th with Block Connection sends no tunnel bytes and closes its slot.
  • Repeat for Block Domain, asserting the offender and all existing same-domain slots close, while unrelated domains remain active.
  • Assert Block All still closes all slots and Notify still permits relay.
  • Fill the JA4 baseline and trigger Block Connection and Block Domain with a 17th distinct accepted ClientHello; assert the offender closes and cannot relay more bytes.
  • Assert Block Domain also closes current sibling tunnels and refuses subsequent CONNECT attempts.
  • Seed 16 JA4 fingerprints, send a 17th accepted Hello plus buffered following bytes to a writable loopback upstream, and assert no bytes arrive when any JA4 Block scope is configured.
  • With a full JA4 baseline, exercise a valid distinct ClientHello against a connected upstream for each Block scope and assert the offending socket closes and sends no tunnel bytes.
  • Verify notify and ignore keep their documented behavior and existing allowlist/SNI checks still apply.
  • With 16 distinct baseline fingerprints, send a 17th valid ClientHello and assert Block Connection closes that socket before the upstream receives bytes.
  • Repeat for Block Domain, asserting the triggering and other matching tunnels close while future CONNECTs are rejected.
  • Repeat for Block All and assert no buffered post-hello payload is sent before the global latch.
  • For Block Domain, verify the triggering and other current same-domain tunnels close while unrelated domains continue.
  • With 16 seeded fingerprints, verify a seventeenth distinct valid JA4 under connection Block closes the offender without upstream bytes.
  • Repeat under fqdn Block and verify the offender, sibling tunnels, and future CONNECTs are denied.
  • Verify All Block and Notify/Ignore still behave as configured.
  • Seed sixteen distinct JA4 values for one ordinal, trigger an overflow under Block Connection, and assert the offender sends no further upstream bytes and is closed.
  • Repeat under Block Domain; assert the triggering and sibling current tunnels close and later admissions are refused.
  • Confirm Block All still stops all application I/O and Notify still permits the validated tunnel.
  • After 16 baseline fingerprints, a new valid JA4 under connection block must send no hello bytes upstream and close its slot.
  • Under fqdn block, the triggering and other active matching slots must close, while future matching CONNECTs are refused.
  • With a full JA4 baseline and Block All, a new valid hello plus coalesced trailing bytes must cause zero upstream writes before closure.
  • Assert the permitted Notify case still forwards the validated hello and trailing data in order.
  • With a full JA4 row and block configured, send a changed ClientHello plus trailing bytes and assert the upstream receives zero bytes.
  • Cover partial writes and pipelined ClientHello bytes.
  • With a full JA4 row, assert Block Connection closes the triggering socket before relay can continue.
  • Assert Block Domain closes the triggering socket and all active same-ordinal sockets, and refuses later same-ordinal CONNECTs.
  • With a full JA4 baseline and a Block All threshold crossing, send a ClientHello with coalesced trailing bytes to a writable upstream; assert zero pre-decision bytes, including when partial writes would otherwise occur.
  • Fill a JA4 row with 16 distinct accepted values, then assert a 17th value with Block Connection closes the offender before relay.
  • Repeat with Block Domain and assert the offender, siblings and future same-ordinal connections are blocked.
  • Verify Notify and Ignore preserve the intended relay behavior and Block All still closes every slot.

Preventive controls:

  • Centralize effect application so every Block scope has an explicit current-slot outcome.
  • Make action projection return a typed continue-or-close decision that every event-loop caller must handle before forwarding.
  • Centralize physical closure for every Block effect and make the triggering slot an explicit operand of scoped enforcement.
  • Test JA4 actions through the real serving path, including the triggering slot and upstream byte count.
  • Centralize block-effect application so every Block scope explicitly handles the triggering slot before relay begins.
  • Make each per-FQDN block action explicitly close the triggering slot in the common tripwire path.
  • Assert policy decisions precede the first upstream write for JA4-triggered blocks.
  • Keep policy decision ordering adjacent to the gate transition that authorizes upstream writes.
  • Keep policy decisions that can reject a connection before effectful socket writes.
  • Make each Block effect's required current-slot termination explicit in one enforcement path.
  • Centralize scoped Block application so every action path enforces the triggering connection as well as broader latches.

Field Value
Severity medium
Confidence medium
Confidence rationale Static control flow and a prequeued-client rearm test support the missing pause guard and missing poll deadline. No injected accept-error runtime reproduction, deployment descriptor limit, or poll-backend timing was established.
Category Listener availability after transient accept failure
CWE CWE-400
Affected lines src/runtime/reactor.rs:1898-1901, src/runtime/reactor.rs:1876-1889, src/runtime/reactor.rs:1320-1344, src/runtime/reactor.rs:1536-1543, src/runtime/reactor.rs:3272-3303, src/runtime/owner.rs:398-400, src/runtime/reactor/tests.rs:5069

Summary

After a non-WouldBlock accept error, the reactor saves a 100 ms listener pause but neither blocks another accept during that pause nor includes its deadline in the poll timeout. Repeated listener readiness can retry the failing accept immediately; if a readiness edge is consumed and the owner then polls quietly, already queued clients can wait well beyond 100 ms for an unrelated wake before the listener is rearmed.

Root Cause

The accept error stores a pause timestamp, but listener readiness remains dispatchable without a pause guard, and poll_timeout omits that timestamp. Rearm occurs only at the start of a later turn, so neither a bounded retry cadence nor a guaranteed wake at 100 ms is enforced.

Field Value
Severity medium

Affected lines src/runtime/reactor.rs:2897, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2415, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2371, src/enforcement/state.rs:351, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2476, src/runtime/reactor.rs:3158, src/config/mod.rs:1006, docs/alumina-proxy.md:309

After a domain’s 16 JA4 baseline slots are full, a client can trigger a JA4 Block with a new valid fingerprint. maybe_record_ja4_baseline() ignores the returned effect; Connection scope never closes the slot, and Domain scope closes siblings but explicitly skips the trigger. maybe_record_ja4_baseline projects a JA4 overflow but discards the effect. project_tripwire handles All by closing every slot; it has no Connection close branch, and the Domain helper receives the triggering index as an exclusion. The Domain bit affects later CONNECT decisions, while the current slot remains in relay and continues I/O.

Configured block semantics — docs/alumina-proxy.md:307-312

The documented contract requires Connection to terminate the offender and Domain to affect current flows.

### Block and Notify semantics

- **Block Connection:** terminates the offender connection only; no scope history.
- **Block Domain:** a fixed ordinal table (at most 32 entries) marks the configured domain blocked; it affects current and future flows matching that ordinal until restart.
- **Block All:** synchronously prevents all subsequent application I/O, including pending writes and new admission, before any further I/O, then performs bounded physical closure of at most 512 slots. It persists until restart; there is no runtime unblock interface.
- **Notify** (renamed from `flare_only`): a notification and aggregation context only. It never authorizes forwarding, never delays baseline denial, and never widens scope. Implicit Notify for an applied Block inherits that Block's scope (reporting scope equals enforcement scope).

Validation

A full JA4 row triggers project_tripwire; configured Block Connection returns without closing the current slot, and Block Domain calls a helper that skips it. The only blocked-domain test in this path is on a new CONNECT. All-scope Block does close the current slot; EarlyUpstreamData has a separate mandatory close.

Severity

Medium — A compromised client can intentionally fill the 16-entry baseline and then trigger a configured Connection or Domain block while using an approved upstream. The missing closure defeats the configured response for that active tunnel, but future Domain connections are blocked and the destination remains limited to the allowlist.

Raise severity if a deployed Block Domain policy is relied on to stop long-lived exfiltration through approved endpoints; lower it if JA4 is Notify or Ignore only, or the triggering tunnel is independently closed in a changed implementation.

Impact assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: Configured current-connection block is not enforced on the trigger; Domain blocks siblings and future connections only.

Likelihood assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: The client must deliberately create 17 distinct valid JA4 fingerprints, but can control ClientHello fields.

Remediation

When a JA4 overflow yields Block Connection or Block Domain, close the triggering slot immediately; for Domain, close it as well as sibling slots and retain the domain latch. Ensure this applies before any further relay I/O.

Tests:

  • Seed 16 distinct JA4 values, trigger a 17th under Block Connection, and assert the offending slot closes.
  • Repeat under Block Domain with an existing sibling tunnel; assert both the trigger and sibling close and later CONNECT is forbidden.
  • Verify Notify and Ignore continue normally, and Block All still closes every slot.

Preventive controls:

  • Centralize effect application so every Block scope has an explicit current-slot disposition.

[12] Test-module gate can certify production unsafe code

Field Value
Severity medium
Confidence high
Confidence rationale The AWK comment match was previously checked in isolation, and the new scan directly traces the file-enumeration gap, symlink admission, path exemption, and docs selector. No modified-source build was performed.
Category Security verification bypass
CWE CWE-693
Affected lines scripts/verify.sh:843-880, scripts/verify.sh:921-979, scripts/verify.sh:1813, docs/verification.md:29, scripts/verify.sh:843-880, scripts/verify.sh:932-979, scripts/verify.sh:1813, scripts/verify.sh:934, scripts/verify.sh:896, scripts/verify.sh:872, scripts/verify.sh:1813, src/runtime/tunnel.rs:964, scripts/verify.sh:870-880, scripts/verify.sh:959-973

Summary

The docs verifier can falsely certify test-only unsafe confinement for a production-compiled src/*/tests.rs or dot_tests.rs module in three source-change cases. Its raw-line AWK check accepts a commented #[cfg(test)] declaration before a bare production declaration; it also accepts a genuine #[cfg(test)] declaration without rejecting a second #[cfg(not(test))] production declaration of the same file. Separately, find -type f omits a resolving symlinked test module accepted by the source inventory. Because the unsafe scanner exempts these paths by filename, each case can print CFG-TEST-PARENTAGE-OK and UNSAFE-SURFACE-OK while production includes unsafe code.

Root Cause

The gate does not validate every effective production module declaration for every admitted test-named Rust path. Raw text can match comments, a first valid test declaration can mask a second production declaration, and -type f skips admitted symlink leaves. The unsafe exemption then trusts the filename without proving the module is excluded from production.

Parentage check scans raw lines — scripts/verify.sh:958-973

This regex accepts matching lines within Rust block comments and stops searching after its first match.

decl=$(awk -v stem="$stem" '
    {
        if (!found && $0 ~ ("^[[:space:]]*#\\[cfg\\(test\\)\\][[:space:]]*(pub\\(crate\\)[[:space:]]+)?mod[[:space:]]+" stem "[[:space:]]*;")) { found = 1; next }
        if (!found && $0 ~ /^[[:space:]]*#\[cfg\(test\)\]/) { pending = 1; next }
        if (pending && $0 ~ /^[[:space:]]*$/) next
        if (pending && $0 ~ ("^[[:space:]]*(pub\\(crate\\)[[:space:]]+)?mod[[:space:]]+" stem "[[:space:]]*;")) found = 1
        pending = 0
    }
    END { print (found ? "ok" : "missing") }
' "$parent" 2>&1) || prc=$?

Parentage gate reports success — scripts/verify.sh:979

A false match leads to the pass marker for all admitted unit modules.

echo "CFG-TEST-PARENTAGE-OK: every admitted src/*/tests.rs and src/*/dot_tests.rs is #[cfg(test)]-declared by its parent"

Unsafe gate exempts test filenames — scripts/verify.sh:869-880

The unsafe gate trusts the path name once a separate parentage check passes.

for f in $offenders; do
    case "$f" in
        src/alloc.rs|tests/*|src/*/tests.rs|src/*/dot_tests.rs) ;;
        *) bad="$bad $f" ;;
    esac
done
if [ -n "$bad" ]; then
    echo "UNSAFE-SURFACE-FAIL: 'unsafe' outside allowlist (prod surface: src/alloc.rs, tests/*; cfg(test) unit modules: src/*/tests.rs, src/*/dot_tests.rs):$bad" >&2
    exit 1
fi

Parentage check scans raw lines — scripts/verify.sh:958-973

This regex accepts matching lines within Rust block comments and stops searching after its first match.

decl=$(awk -v stem="$stem" '
    {
        if (!found && $0 ~ ("^[[:space:]]*#\\[cfg\\(test\\)\\][[:space:]]*(pub\\(crate\\)[[:space:]]+)?mod[[:space:]]+" stem "[[:space:]]*;")) { found = 1; next }
        if (!found && $0 ~ /^[[:space:]]*#\[cfg\(test\)\]/) { pending = 1; next }
        if (pending && $0 ~ /^[[:space:]]*$/) next
        if (pending && $0 ~ ("^[[:space:]]*(pub\\(crate\\)[[:space:]]+)?mod[[:space:]]+" stem "[[:space:]]*;")) found = 1
        pending = 0
    }
    END { print (found ? "ok" : "missing") }
' "$parent" 2>&1) || prc=$?

Documented local security gate — docs/verification.md:29

The repository presents the selector as a parentage and unsafe-surface verification gate.

Severity

Medium — Two independently reachable source-change cases can produce a false pass from the documented local security verification gate and allow unsafe code in a production-compiled module outside the approved surface. Both require contributor control and review or workflow reliance on the gate; no CI consumer or production deployment was established. The earlier aggregate rated the commented-declaration case low on that basis.

Severity rises if a release or PR workflow treats the gate as authoritative for untrusted contributions; it falls if reviewers or independent compiler-aware checks establish the module graph.

Impact assessment:

  • Level: low
  • Why: The false verification result can conceal production unsafe code from this one local control, while changed source remains visible to review.

Likelihood assessment:

  • Level: low
  • Why: Requires crafted source edits and an independently trusted use of the local gate.

Remediation

Enumerate every admitted test-named Rust module, including resolving symlink leaves, and validate every actual declaration with Rust syntax or compiler cfg-expanded metadata. Reject commented-only matches, any additional production or ambiguous declaration, and unguarded module paths before reporting the unsafe-surface pass. Rejecting test-module symlinks is an alternative for the symlink case, but every regular-file declaration still needs checking.

Tests:

  • Place a commented cfg(test)/mod tests pair before a bare production mod tests; and require the docs gate to fail.
  • Verify genuine cfg(test) unit modules continue to pass, including single-line and two-line forms.
  • Place a commented #[cfg(test)] mod tests; beside a bare mod tests; and assert the docs gate fails.
  • Keep an actual #[cfg(test)] mod tests; case and assert the gate passes.
  • Create a temporary symlinked src/runtime/tests.rs resolving to a regular file, remove its parent's cfg(test), and assert the docs gate fails.
  • Verify a regular guarded tests.rs still passes and broken symlinks fail.
  • Give a parent both #[cfg(test)] mod tests; and #[cfg(not(test))] mod tests;, with unsafe in tests.rs, and assert the docs gate fails.

Preventive controls:

  • Treat filename exemptions as conditional on parsed or compiler-derived module reachability.
  • Make unsafe-file exemptions depend on parsed module inclusion instead of path spelling.
  • Check all effective cfg branches for each exempt test-named module, including alternate declarations of the same file.

Affected lines src/runtime/reactor.rs:2853, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2416, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2371, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2897, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2847-2854, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2886-2898, src/enforcement/policy.rs:129-155, src/enforcement/state.rs:347-369, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2405-2427, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2921-2973, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2853-2854, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2415-2427, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2371-2381, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2885-2898, src/enforcement/state.rs:351-368, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2921-2989, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2825-2854, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2881-2898, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2921-3015, src/runtime/reactor/reject.rs:79-99, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2405-2429, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2371-2380, src/enforcement/state.rs:351-372, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2886-2902, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2975-3019, src/config/mod.rs:1005-1014, src/runtime/reactor.rs:605-619, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2883-2899, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2975-3015, src/enforcement/state.rs:351-369

Summary

After 16 distinct JA4 fingerprints fill an allowed domain’s baseline, a client can send a 17th valid fingerprint on an allowlisted CONNECT. The reactor forwards the validated ClientHello and potentially buffered trailing bytes before evaluating the configured JA4 block. Block Connection records an effect but never closes the triggering slot; Block Domain latches the domain and closes other matching slots while exempting the offender. The triggering slot can advance to Relay and continue upstream exchange. Block All closes slots after the decision, so bytes forwarded before that decision remain a timing consequence of the same order.

Root Cause

The JA4 block decision follows the first upstream flush of the validated ClientHello and potentially buffered trailing bytes. If that write closes the slot, inspector reset can suppress recording the change. Once overflow is projected, Connection scope has no offender-close branch and Domain scope closes matching siblings while exempting the triggering slot; the active slot can enter Relay. Block All closes slots after its decision but cannot retract bytes already sent.

const fn apply_per_fqdn_action(&mut self, effect: Effect, ordinal: DomainOrdinal) {
    match effect {
        Effect::Notify { .. } => {
            self.monitor.note_action_notify(ordinal);
        }
        Effect::Block { scope } => {
            self.monitor.note_action_domain_block(ordinal);
            match scope {
                Scope::Domain => self.blocked |= 1 << ordinal.get(),
                Scope::All => {
                    let was_latched = self.block_all;
                    self.block_all = true;

  • Connection and Domain block effects leave the triggering slot open.
  • All scope closes the triggering slot and is not affected.
  • The 16-entry baseline returns Overflow for the next distinct fingerprint.

Counterevidence and remaining uncertainty:

  • The CONNECT host and TLS SNI still must match the allowlist; the flaw affects a configured JA4 block, not general destination authorization.
  • Block All closes all slots after its threshold, but the first upstream write may already have occurred.
  • Exact CONNECT hostname and port authorization still applies; the bypass does not grant arbitrary egress.
  • Block(All) closes slots after the JA4 decision, limiting that scope to bytes forwarded before the decision.
  • Only an exact allowlisted pair and successfully validated ClientHello reaches this path (src/runtime/reactor.rs:2450-2522,2825-2850).
  • The first 16 distinct JA4 values seed the baseline (src/runtime/reactor.rs:600-619).

  • Change signal requires a full 16-entry baseline and is suppressed by Ignore (src/runtime/reactor.rs:600-619,2891-2901).

const fn apply_per_fqdn_action(&mut self, effect: Effect, ordinal: DomainOrdinal) {
    match effect {
        Effect::Notify { .. } => {
            self.monitor.note_action_notify(ordinal);
        }
        Effect::Block { scope } => {
            self.monitor.note_action_domain_block(ordinal);
            match scope {
                Scope::Domain => self.blocked |= 1 << ordinal.get(),
                Scope::All => {
                    let was_latched = self.block_all;
                    self.block_all = true;
                    if !was_latched {
                        self.monitor.note_block_all();
                    }
                }
                Scope::Connection => {}
            }
        }

Reachability

Requires listener access, an approved CONNECT hostname and port with a current eligible DNS binding and matching valid SNI, a configured JA4 Block Connection or Domain policy, and 16 distinct accepted fingerprints for the same domain ordinal. The 17th distinct fingerprint triggers the block while the initiating tunnel can continue relaying.

  • Attacker: compromised application client with listener access

  • Entry point: CONNECT and initial TLS ClientHello

  • Outcome: continued traffic on the triggering tunnel after the block

Preconditions:

  • Proxy is deployed and reachable by the adversarial workload.
  • An allowlisted domain has JA4 configured to block at connection or domain scope.
  • The per-ordinal baseline contains 16 distinct fingerprints; the next is new.
  • An allowed hostname and current eligible DNS binding exist.
  • The operator configured ja4 block with connection or domain scope.
  • The attacker can send enough distinct valid ClientHello variants to fill the 16-value baseline.
  • Allowlisted FQDN:port and eligible DNS binding
  • JA4 block configured for the allowlist entry
  • 16 distinct accepted JA4 fingerprints previously seeded for that ordinal

Existing controls:

  • Exact CONNECT allowlist and matching SNI still apply.
  • All-scope block closes all slots.
  • Domain scope blocks future and other current flows.
  • The CONNECT host and TLS SNI still must match the allowlist; this is a JA4 policy bypass rather than general destination authorization.
  • Exact allowlist pair and SNI/TLS profile check still hold.
  • Block All works; Domain latch blocks future connections.

Severity

Medium — A client can continue traffic on an approved-destination tunnel the operator explicitly configured to block. The client must reach the proxy, use an allowlisted CONNECT and matching SNI, and fill the 16-entry JA4 baseline before triggering overflow; the flaw does not authorize arbitrary destinations.

Severity rises if approved endpoints provide sensitive attacker-usable capabilities and JA4 blocks are relied on to stop that traffic; it falls if JA4 action is Notify or the listener is unreachable to an attacker.

Impact assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: The security tripwire fails to terminate the anomalous flow, but the destination remains restricted to the approved endpoint.

Likelihood assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: After baseline saturation, the control-flow bypass is deterministic; setup and configuration prerequisites narrow exposure.

Remediation

Evaluate and record JA4 overflow immediately after ClientHello validation, before flushing the Hello or any buffered trailing bytes. Apply the configured action before upstream I/O and retain the change signal if a subsequent write fails. Close the triggering slot for Block Connection and Block Domain; for Domain also close siblings and latch future matching flows, and for All close all slots. Make the caller stop processing a closed slot.

Tests:

  • Configure JA4 Block Connection; saturate one ordinal's baseline and verify the triggering slot closes before any upstream write.
  • Repeat with JA4 Block Domain and verify the triggering slot, sibling flows, and future flows are blocked.
  • Confirm Notify and All actions retain their intended behavior.
  • With ja4 = { action = "block", scope = "connection" }, fill the baseline and verify the 17th distinct ClientHello closes its own tunnel before bytes reach upstream.
  • With scope = "fqdn", verify the triggering and sibling tunnels close and later CONNECT requests for that ordinal are refused.
  • With scope = "all", verify no pending client bytes are sent after the block decision.
  • Seed 16 distinct accepted JA4s, configure Block All, send a 17th fingerprint with pipelined application bytes, and assert no bytes reach upstream before the block.
  • Force an upstream write failure and assert the JA4 change signal is still retained.
  • Seed 16 distinct JA4 fingerprints, trigger a 17th under Block Connection, and assert the current tunnel closes before relay.
  • Repeat under Block Domain and assert both the triggering and other current matching tunnels close, while future matching CONNECT requests are refused.
  • Verify Block All and notify/ignore behavior remain correct.
  • After seeding 16 distinct JA4s, assert a 17th with Block Connection sends no tunnel bytes and closes its slot.
  • Repeat for Block Domain, asserting the offender and all existing same-domain slots close, while unrelated domains remain active.
  • Assert Block All still closes all slots and Notify still permits relay.
  • Fill the JA4 baseline and trigger Block Connection and Block Domain with a 17th distinct accepted ClientHello; assert the offender closes and cannot relay more bytes.
  • Assert Block Domain also closes current sibling tunnels and refuses subsequent CONNECT attempts.
  • Seed 16 JA4 fingerprints, send a 17th accepted Hello plus buffered following bytes to a writable loopback upstream, and assert no bytes arrive when any JA4 Block scope is configured.

Preventive controls:

  • Centralize effect application so every Block scope has an explicit current-slot outcome.
  • Make action projection return a typed continue-or-close decision that every event-loop caller must handle before forwarding.
  • Centralize physical closure for every Block effect and make the triggering slot an explicit operand of scoped enforcement.

Summary

After 16 distinct JA4 fingerprints fill an allowed domain’s baseline, a client can send a 17th valid fingerprint on an allowlisted CONNECT. The reactor forwards the validated ClientHello and potentially buffered trailing bytes before evaluating the configured JA4 block. Block Connection records an effect but never closes the triggering slot; Block Domain latches the domain and closes other matching slots while exempting the offender. The triggering slot can advance to Relay and continue upstream exchange. Block All closes slots after the decision, so bytes forwarded before that decision remain a timing consequence of the same order.

Root Cause

The JA4 block decision follows the first upstream flush of the validated ClientHello and potentially buffered trailing bytes. If that write closes the slot, inspector reset can suppress recording the change. Once overflow is projected, Connection scope has no offender-close branch and Domain scope closes matching siblings while exempting the triggering slot; the active slot can enter Relay. Block All closes slots after its decision but cannot retract bytes already sent.

The specified scope semantics include the current triggering flow.

- **Block Domain:** a fixed ordinal table (at most 32 entries) marks the configured domain blocked; it affects current and future flows matching that ordinal until restart.

  • JA4 overflow is reachable after 16 distinct fingerprints for one approved ordinal.
  • Connection and Domain block effects leave the triggering slot open.
  • All scope closes the triggering slot and is not affected.
  • The 16-entry baseline returns Overflow for the next distinct fingerprint.
  • The configured ja4 action can be block with connection or fqdn scope.
  • The triggering slot is omitted from both closure branches and can remain in relay.
  • A failed first upstream write can reset the inspector before the later JA4 lookup records the change.

Counterevidence and remaining uncertainty:

  • The CONNECT host and TLS SNI still must match the allowlist; the flaw affects a configured JA4 block, not general destination authorization.
  • Block All closes all slots after its threshold, but the first upstream write may already have occurred.
  • Exact CONNECT hostname and port authorization still applies; the bypass does not grant arbitrary egress.
  • Block(All) closes slots after the JA4 decision, limiting that scope to bytes forwarded before the decision.
  • Only an exact allowlisted pair and successfully validated ClientHello reaches this path (src/runtime/reactor.rs:2450-2522,2825-2850).
  • The first 16 distinct JA4 values seed the baseline (src/runtime/reactor.rs:600-619).
  • The proxy relays to an approved endpoint and does not decrypt later payloads (README.md:22-25,48-50).
  • Block All closes live slots through src/runtime/reactor.rs:2355-2365.
  • Domain latch blocks later matching CONNECT at src/runtime/reactor.rs:2473-2481.
  • Change signal requires a full 16-entry baseline and is suppressed by Ignore (src/runtime/reactor.rs:600-619,2891-2901).

Limitations:

  • No runtime reproduction was run.
  • Real-world impact depends on an actual listener, configured JA4 Block action, and capabilities of an approved endpoint.
  • Block All closes the triggering slot, although its first ClientHello write may have preceded the verdict.
  • Validated by source review without executing the proxy; no deployment configuration was supplied.
  • No runtime reproduction or actual operator configuration was supplied.

Reachability

Requires listener access, an approved CONNECT hostname and port with a current eligible DNS binding and matching valid SNI, a configured JA4 Block Connection or Domain policy, and 16 distinct accepted fingerprints for the same domain ordinal. The 17th distinct fingerprint triggers the block while the initiating tunnel can continue relaying.

  • Attacker: compromised application client with listener access

  • Entry point: CONNECT and initial TLS ClientHello

  • Outcome: continued traffic on the triggering tunnel after the block

Preconditions:

  • Proxy is deployed and reachable by the adversarial workload.
  • An allowlisted domain has JA4 configured to block at connection or domain scope.
  • The per-ordinal baseline contains 16 distinct fingerprints; the next is new.
  • An allowed hostname and current eligible DNS binding exist.
  • The operator configured ja4 block with connection or domain scope.
  • The attacker can send enough distinct valid ClientHello variants to fill the 16-value baseline.
  • Allowlisted FQDN:port and eligible DNS binding
  • JA4 block configured for the allowlist entry
  • 16 distinct accepted JA4 fingerprints previously seeded for that ordinal

Existing controls:

  • Exact CONNECT allowlist and matching SNI still apply.
  • All-scope block closes all slots.
  • Domain scope blocks future and other current flows.
  • The CONNECT host and TLS SNI still must match the allowlist; this is a JA4 policy bypass rather than general destination authorization.
  • Exact allowlist pair and SNI/TLS profile check still hold.
  • Block All works; Domain latch blocks future connections.

Severity

Medium — A client can continue traffic on an approved-destination tunnel the operator explicitly configured to block. The client must reach the proxy, use an allowlisted CONNECT and matching SNI, and fill the 16-entry JA4 baseline before triggering overflow; the flaw does not authorize arbitrary destinations.

Severity rises if approved endpoints provide sensitive attacker-usable capabilities and JA4 blocks are relied on to stop that traffic; it falls if JA4 action is Notify or the listener is unreachable to an attacker.

Impact assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: The security tripwire fails to terminate the anomalous flow, but the destination remains restricted to the approved endpoint.

Likelihood assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: After baseline saturation, the control-flow bypass is deterministic; setup and configuration prerequisites narrow exposure.

Remediation

Evaluate and record JA4 overflow immediately after ClientHello validation, before flushing the Hello or any buffered trailing bytes. Apply the configured action before upstream I/O and retain the change signal if a subsequent write fails. Close the triggering slot for Block Connection and Block Domain; for Domain also close siblings and latch future matching flows, and for All close all slots. Make the caller stop processing a closed slot.

Tests:

  • Configure JA4 Block Connection; saturate one ordinal's baseline and verify the triggering slot closes before any upstream write.
  • Repeat with JA4 Block Domain and verify the triggering slot, sibling flows, and future flows are blocked.
  • Confirm Notify and All actions retain their intended behavior.
  • With ja4 = { action = "block", scope = "connection" }, fill the baseline and verify the 17th distinct ClientHello closes its own tunnel before bytes reach upstream.
  • With scope = "fqdn", verify the triggering and sibling tunnels close and later CONNECT requests for that ordinal are refused.
  • With scope = "all", verify no pending client bytes are sent after the block decision.
  • Seed 16 distinct accepted JA4s, configure Block All, send a 17th fingerprint with pipelined application bytes, and assert no bytes reach upstream before the block.
  • Force an upstream write failure and assert the JA4 change signal is still retained.
  • Seed 16 distinct JA4 fingerprints, trigger a 17th under Block Connection, and assert the current tunnel closes before relay.
  • Repeat under Block Domain and assert both the triggering and other current matching tunnels close, while future matching CONNECT requests are refused.
  • Verify Block All and notify/ignore behavior remain correct.

Preventive controls:

  • Centralize effect application so every Block scope has an explicit current-slot outcome.
  • Make action projection return a typed continue-or-close decision that every event-loop caller must handle before forwarding.

[15] Reopened DNS incident reports a prior family failure

Field Value
Severity low
Confidence high
Confidence rationale Source trace shows close_window preserves snapshots and note_incident_open overwrites only Some entries on reopen.
Category Security telemetry integrity
CWE CWE-778
Affected lines src/dns/incident_report.rs:321-342, src/dns/incident_report.rs:467-481, src/runtime/storage.rs:784-828, src/dns/incident_report.rs:98-109, src/dns/incident_report.rs:473, src/dns/incident_report.rs:321, src/dns/incident_report.rs:102, src/runtime/storage.rs:784

Summary

After a DNS incident fully recovers, the report closes its window but retains the old A and AAAA snapshots. A later incident affecting only one family before timed rotation overwrites only that family's snapshot, so the new summary can attribute the other family's old start time, reason, and resolver to the new incident. Both A-then-AAAA and AAAA-then-A sequences are affected; DNS cache admission and destination selection do not use this report state.

Root Cause

The incident state persists across full-recovery window closure, while reopening updates only present family snapshots. Full-recovery close leaves the per-family incident array intact; only hourly rotation clears it.

Reopen preserves absent family — src/dns/incident_report.rs:321-342

An absent current family snapshot leaves the previously stored value intact even for a newly opened window.

let nr = &mut self.names[name];
if let Some((opened_at, reason, origin)) = incident[0] {
    nr.incident[0] = Some((opened_at, reason, origin));
}
if let Some((opened_at, reason, origin)) = incident[1] {
    nr.incident[1] = Some((opened_at, reason, origin));
}
if nr.window_open {
    return;
}
nr.window_open = true;
nr.window_start = now;
nr.reset_window_counters();

Full recovery leaves old snapshots — src/dns/incident_report.rs:467-481

Closing captures the final summary but does not clear nr.incident.

if !nr.window_open {
    return None;
}
nr.window_open = false;

Summary

A peer that can reach the listener can hold 128 incomplete CONNECT requests until their ten-second setup deadlines. Once the pending pool is full, the proxy rejects other clients with HTTP 503. The listener admits all peers into a single pending setup pool. A short incomplete CONNECT head remains in setup, and admission checks only global counters, so one reachable peer can occupy every pending slot before other clients arrive.

Summary

Native Rust log and startup test sinks use predictable PID/counter paths and nonexclusive truncating opens. The boot fixture accepts a planted PID/counter directory and writes config.toml through a planted child link. The shutdown E2E script independently truncates fixed /tmp/shutdown-{name}.log paths. The documented host benchmark self-test defaults to shared /tmp: its B8 probe unconditionally truncates /tmp/seam_shell8.out, while TLS branches write fixed key, certificate, and config names such as /tmp/ext.cnf. Each path can modify a runner-writable file if local co-tenancy and filesystem policy permit it; production serving does not call these helpers. Even a custom --selftest-tmp does not relocate B8's absolute /tmp/seam_shell8.out path. The ext.cnf case specifically requires a TLS 1.3 capable host: the selftest reaches _run_proxyless, calls _gen_ca_and_cert, and opens the fixed /tmp/ext.cnf path with Python's truncating open(..., 'w'). A separate local user can preplant the symlink; the written certificate-extension line is fixed, and the documented LibreSSL host skips this TLS branch.

Root Cause

Test and benchmark helpers assume predictable shared temporary paths are private. Rust helpers reuse PID/counter directories or nonexclusively truncate sink files; the host benchmark uses fixed /tmp names, including an unconditional shell redirection. None establishes a private owned namespace and refuses attacker-planted links before writing. The shutdown E2E test also opens a public fixed /tmp log name with wb, without exclusive creation or a private directory. The B8 absolute path remains in shared /tmp even when --selftest-tmp selects another directory. The TLS-capable branch passes the selected tmpdir to certificate generation, where ext.cnf is opened in truncating, symlink-following mode; a custom shared --selftest-tmp requires the same ownership and exclusive-creation protection.

Predictable log test path and truncating open — src/log/tests.rs:21-35

The filename is derived from a process ID and sequential counter; the open follows an existing symlink and truncates its target.

    ));

def _gen_ca_and_cert(tmpdir):
    ca_key = os.path.join(tmpdir, "ca.key")
    ca_pem = os.path.join(tmpdir, "ca.pem")
    key = os.path.join(tmpdir, "server.key")
    csr = os.path.join(tmpdir, "server.csr")
    pem = os.path.join(tmpdir, "server.pem")
    subprocess.run(["openssl", "req", "-x509", "-newkey", "rsa:2048",
                    "-keyout", ca_key, "-out", ca_pem, "-days", "2", "-nodes",
                    "-subj", "/CN=bench-ca"],
                   check=True, capture_output=True)
    subprocess.run(["openssl", "req", "-newkey", "rsa:2048", "-keyout", key,
                    "-out", csr, "-days", "2", "-nodes", "-subj", "/CN=example.com"],
                   check=True, capture_output=True)
    with open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "ext.cnf"), "w") as fh:
        fh.write("subjectAltName=DNS:example.com\n")
    subprocess.run(["openssl", "x509", "-req", "-in", csr, "-CA", ca_pem,
                    "-CAkey", ca_key, "-CAcreateserial", "-out", pem, "-days", "1",
                    "-extfile", os.path.join(tmpdir, "ext.cnf")],

Both truncating test sink helpers use predictable paths, and the boot helper accepts an existing predictable directory before writing a child config.toml. Each is reachable through the corresponding native tests. Local exploitability depends on shared temporary storage and runner filesystem rights. The documented host benchmark adds independently reachable fixed /tmp writes, including an unconditional B8 output truncation and TLS certificate/config paths; this requires the same shared-host authority boundary. The latest trace identifies the supported native boot selectors and a second config.toml fixture write; the boot directory's nested link can remain effective where sticky-directory protections block a direct /tmp link. The shutdown E2E script adds separately reachable fixed-name /tmp log truncation when its cases execute on a shared host. The assigned worker independently confirmed the boot fixture path and both distinct Rust log sinks, including their PID/counter naming and nonexclusive writes. The assigned worker independently corroborated the boot fixture, both Rust log sinks, and the benchmark paths, including fixed key and config names. This worker also identified a non-UTF-8 boot test that rewrites the same config.toml child path after creating the fixture. The assigned review independently confirms the boot fixture, both predictable truncating Rust log sinks, and the host benchmark's fixed TLS artifact paths; the separate owner test helper uses exclusive creation. The newly assigned trace confirms that the TLS 1.3 capable selftest path reaches _gen_ca_and_cert and its fixed ext.cnf truncating write; the documented LibreSSL host skips this branch.

Assertions:

  • scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:810 and :1252 truncate fixed-name files in /tmp during e2e tests.
  • The directory name is derived from fixed tags, PID, and a starting counter.
  • The helper accepts a preexisting directory and writes config.toml within it.
  • The sink name uses PID and a counter starting at zero.
  • The open requests create and truncate without exclusive creation.
  • Boot fixture names use fixed tags, PID, and incrementing counter.
  • create_dir_all accepts an existing directory and does not establish exclusive ownership.
  • Boot tests write config.toml beneath that directory.
  • Log test names use PID/counter and open with create plus truncate.
  • Startup integration also opens a PID-and-counter log filename with create plus truncate, then uses it as a log sink.
  • The directory name includes known tag, process ID and monotonic counter (tests/support/temp_dir.rs:7-13).
  • Existing directories pass through create_dir_all (tests/support/temp_dir.rs:13).
  • fs::write opens and truncates the child path without a no-follow check (tests/support/temp_dir.rs:21-24).
  • The B8 fixture uses an absolute /tmp path even when --selftest-tmp specifies a different workspace.
  • An attacker who can create /tmp/ext.cnf can substitute a symlink before the operator executes the selftest.
  • The write occurs under the selftest operator's filesystem permissions.

Counterevidence and remaining uncertainty:

  • Both affected modules are compiled under cfg(test) (src/log/mod.rs:1041-1042; src/runtime/storage.rs:1672-1675).
  • src/runtime/owner/tests.rs:1116-1134 uses create_new(true), showing a safer sibling pattern.
  • No actual shared test host, higher-privilege runner, or symlink policy was supplied.
  • Only test code uses these helpers.
  • The impact is limited by test-runner filesystem permissions.
  • A private test temp directory prevents cross-user preplanting; Linux protected_symlinks can constrain the direct log-file variant but does not establish ownership of an attacker-created child directory.
  • src/runtime/owner/tests.rs:1116-1134 and src/dns/transport/tests.rs:4994-4999 use create_new(true), which rejects existing paths for those helpers.
  • Per-user temporary directories and isolated containers remove the cross-user preplacement capability.
  • The authoritative benchmark self-test is also documented inside a container, which removes this cross-user host scenario when isolated.
  • Linux sticky-directory protected-symlink settings may block cross-user following; the documented macOS host path and unusual shared-host settings still need their own controls.
  • The production binary does not call these test helpers.
  • Other test sink helpers use create_new(true), which refuses preexisting paths (src/runtime/owner/tests.rs:1116-1133; src/dns/transport/tests.rs:4994-4999).
  • Some Linux shared temporary directories enable protected symlink rules that may block the direct log-file variant.
  • The affected operations run only in test code, not the production proxy.
  • A private temporary root or inability to predict the name prevents the attack.
  • The test-controlled content is fixed; the attacker selects the target, not arbitrary bytes.
  • The direct log-file symlink variant may be blocked by host sticky-directory symlink protections; the precreated boot subdirectory has a different parent-directory ownership path.
  • The attacker does not control arbitrary file content; fixture bytes are fixed by tests.
  • The helper is used by tests, not the production proxy.
  • A single-user or isolated CI temp directory removes the lower-trust local attacker prerequisite.
  • The documented LibreSSL host skips TLS-dependent checks, while TLS-capable host Python and the documented container execute them.
  • Modern sticky-directory symlink protections may block cross-user following on some hosts.

Limitations:

  • No runtime exploit attempted; host-specific symlink protections and test-runner permissions are unknown.
  • No runtime reproduction or host temp policy verification was performed.
  • No runtime reproduction was performed; actual CI temporary-directory permissions and test runner privilege are unknown.
  • No shared-host runtime proof was performed.
  • Actual CI/local test runner permissions are unknown.
  • The repository does not establish that tests run on a shared multiuser host or under a more privileged account.
  • No symlink attack was executed.
  • The repository does not establish a shared multiuser test host or privileged test runner.
  • The issue is test-only and was not reproduced at runtime.
  • No runtime symlink reproduction was run.
  • Actual test-runner TMPDIR isolation and privileges are unknown.
  • Host symlink-following protections were not established from repository source.
  • No live race or filesystem reproduction was run.
  • No dynamic exploit or environment-specific permission test was run.

An attacker can preplace /tmp/ext.cnf as a symlink. open(..., 'w') follows it and truncates the runner-writable target; the other generated artifacts also use fixed names.

def _gen_ca_and_cert(tmpdir):
    ca_key = os.path.join(tmpdir, "ca.key")
    ca_pem = os.path.join(tmpdir, "ca.pem")
    key = os.path.join(tmpdir, "server.key")
    csr = os.path.join(tmpdir, "server.csr")
    pem = os.path.join(tmpdir, "server.pem")
    subprocess.run(["openssl", "req", "-x509", "-newkey", "rsa:2048",
                    "-keyout", ca_key, "-out", ca_pem, "-days", "2", "-nodes",
                    "-subj", "/CN=bench-ca"],
                   check=True, capture_output=True)
    subprocess.run(["openssl", "req", "-newkey", "rsa:2048", "-keyout", key,
                    "-out", csr, "-days", "2", "-nodes", "-subj", "/CN=example.com"],
                   check=True, capture_output=True)
    with open(os.path.join(tmpdir, "ext.cnf"), "w") as fh:
        fh.write("subjectAltName=DNS:example.com\n")

Reachability

Reachable during the relevant native test runs if a local user can preplant or race entries in a shared writable temporary directory. Direct sink links require permitted symlink following; the boot directory variant relies on create_dir_all accepting a pre-existing path and the child write following a planted config.toml link. The documented host benchmark self-test also runs in this boundary when invoked outside its containerized setup. The native boot selector and host-native inner test entry point make the fixture write separately reachable; B8 runs regardless of TLS capability. The shutdown E2E suite opens fixed case log paths through open_case_log; its tests can reach this sink on a shared host. The newly corroborated boot case specifically uses an initial alumina-boot-oversize-<pid>-0 directory with a planted config.toml child link. The ext.cnf path is reached through _run_proxyless only on a TLS 1.3 capable host; the documented LibreSSL host skips this branch, while the unconditional B8 path remains reachable.

  • Attacker: Local co-tenant with access to shared temp storage

  • Entry point: native Rust test fixture/log setup or documented host benchmark self-test or shutdown E2E suite

  • Sink: OpenOptions::open with truncate(true) or fs::write on config.toml or Python open(..., 'wb') on /tmp/shutdown-{name}.log

  • Outcome: Clobber a file writable by the test runner

Preconditions:

  • Tests execute on a shared multi-user host or equivalent shared temp namespace
  • A target file is writable by the runner but protected from the attacker
  • For the boot fixture variant, attacker can plant a directory and nested config.toml link before the native test uses it.
  • For benchmark B8, host self-test runs with shared /tmp and a planted /tmp/seam_shell8.out link.
  • For shutdown E2E logs, a fixed case name is used on a shared host and a runner-writable target is planted at /tmp/shutdown-{name}.log.
  • For ext.cnf, the host selftest reaches the TLS 1.3 branch, another local user can preplant a link in the selected shared directory, and host symlink policy permits following it.
  • Shared writable temp directory
  • Relevant native tests execute
  • Predictable or raced PID/counter path
  • Target file writable by test runner
  • Symlink following allowed for the affected path
  • Shutdown E2E cases execute in a shared /tmp namespace for the fixed-log variant

Log test opens predictable path with truncation — src/log/tests.rs:21-35

A pre-existing symlink at the predictable log path is followed, and the target is truncated when this helper runs.

fn temp_file() -> File {
    static COUNTER: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);
    let mut path = std::env::temp_dir();
    path.push(format!(
        "alumina-log-{}-{}.log",
        std::process::id(),
        COUNTER.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)
    ));
    std::fs::OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .create(true)
        .truncate(true)
        .open(&path)
        .expect("create temp file")

Severity

Low — Local, native-test-only file clobber requires shared writable temporary storage, predictable or raced PID/counter placement, a runner-writable target, and the relevant test execution. Direct sink symlinks also depend on host symlink-following policy; a planted boot fixture directory and child path have a distinct bypass of path ownership.

Private runner temp directories or symlink protections reduce likelihood; a privileged CI runner with shared temp space and predictable test execution raises impact. The benchmark host self-test adds an unconditional fixed /tmp output path; its containerized invocation avoids a cross-user host namespace.

Impact assessment:

  • Level: low
  • Rationale: Conditional integrity loss to runner-writable files; no production proxy network path.

Likelihood assessment:

  • Level: low
  • Rationale: Requires local placement and test timing under permissive host temp policy.

Remediation

Create private, owned, unpredictable temporary directories for native test fixtures, log sinks, shutdown E2E logs, and host benchmark artifacts. Claim files exclusively without following symlinks; reject pre-existing boot fixture directories and child links. Move the shutdown /tmp/shutdown-{name}.log files, unconditional benchmark B8 output, and benchmark TLS key, certificate, and config files under their respective private directories, and clean up only runner-owned resources. For an explicit --selftest-tmp, require an operator-owned private directory and create ext.cnf and other outputs exclusively without following links.

Tests:

  • Precreate a symlink at a candidate temp path and confirm the helper refuses it without changing the target.
  • Run the test suite with concurrent sink creation and verify unique files are created safely.
  • Run tests with a pre-existing symlink and directory at the would-be fixture paths and assert they do not overwrite external files.
  • Preplant a boot fixture directory containing a config.toml symlink and confirm the test helper rejects it without modifying the target.
  • Preplace the expected directory and config.toml symlink, then assert the helper fails without modifying the target.
  • Preplace each log sink filename as a symlink and assert test setup refuses it without truncation.
  • Run the legitimate tests with a private temporary directory and confirm fixture cleanup.
  • Preplace /tmp/ext.cnf as a symlink, run the host self-test with a safe temporary directory, and assert the target is untouched.
  • Preplace /tmp/seam_shell8.out as a symlink and assert the host self-test refuses it without modifying the target.
  • Pre-create the candidate directory with a nested config.toml symlink and assert test setup refuses it without changing the target.
  • Pre-create the direct log-file path or symlink and assert exclusive creation fails without truncation.
  • Pre-create the expected path or a symlink and verify the helper refuses it without modifying the target.
  • Run concurrent test instances to confirm separate private temporary workspaces.
  • Run shutdown E2E cases with a pre-planted fixed-name /tmp log symlink and verify the target is unchanged and the suite uses a private owned workspace.
  • Precreate the candidate directory and config.toml symlink, then assert the helper refuses or chooses a new private directory without touching the linked target.
  • Assert concurrent test runs use distinct private directories and clean up only directories they created.
  • Preplace a symlink at the predicted sink name and assert the helper refuses it or creates a separate safe file without altering the target.
  • Assert concurrent test runs never reuse a log sink path.
  • Preplace a symlink at the predicted log test sink name and assert the helper refuses it or creates a separate safe file without altering the target.
  • Assert concurrent log test runs never reuse a sink path.
  • Precreate a candidate directory or symlink and confirm the helper refuses it rather than writing through it.
  • Verify concurrent tests obtain distinct private fixture paths.
  • Precreate a colliding temp directory with a config.toml symlink and assert the test helper refuses it without touching the symlink target.
  • Verify the replacement helper creates a private directory and cleans up only the directory it owns.
  • Preplant a symlink at the predictable startup log path and assert the replacement helper refuses it without truncating the target.
  • Preplant a symlink at the alumina-log-* path and assert the replacement helper refuses it without truncating the target.
  • Plant a symlink at the default benchmark selftest ext.cnf path and assert the selftest refuses to overwrite its target.
  • Preplant a symlink at the old shared path and verify a default selftest neither reads nor modifies its target.
  • Verify two concurrent default selftests use separate directories and complete without clobbering files.

Preventive controls:

  • Use a shared temporary-resource utility that atomically creates files and directories with private permissions.
  • Use one safe temporary-file helper across tests and avoid predictable PID-only paths.
  • Use one shared secure temporary-directory helper for tests instead of PID-based names and create_dir_all.
  • Centralize test log sink creation in a secure temporary-file helper.
  • Centralize test temporary-file creation in an audited secure helper.
  • Use one secure temporary-directory helper for every test and fixture writer.

[19] Shutdown test can pass after observing an admitted connection

Field Value
Severity low
Confidence high
Confidence rationale The double-probe branch and its call sites are explicit in current source; no runtime timing reproduction was performed.
Category Security verification bypass / shutdown admission
CWE CWE-20, CWE-693
Affected lines scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:147, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:168, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:226, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:1047, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:1204, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:226-239, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:169-183, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:1047, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:1204, scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:1524-1534

Summary

During the shutdown E2E cases, probe_refused_sampled() treats an initial successful post-signal connection as a reason to perform a second probe. If the listener closes between the probes, the second refusal lets the case pass even though the first probe observed the forbidden admission.

Root Cause

The no-admission helper's documentation says a successful connect must fail. Its implementation calls connect_probe() and returns success for refusal, but for a successful connection it calls sample_no_bind(), which probes again. A refusal on that later attempt replaces the earlier success instead of failing the case.

A successful connect is classified reachable — scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:147-165

The first sampled TCP connect returns reachable when it succeeds; this observation should fail the no-admission claim.

def connect_probe():
    """One sampled connect to the proxy port, classified so an observation
    boundary error can never count as listener absence:
      ("reachable", None)  connection accepted (listener reachable/bound)
      ("refused", None)    authoritative connection refusal (no listener)
      ("error", exc)       operational failure (timeout/EMFILE/EACCES/
                           ENETUNREACH/reset/...) - indeterminate, never absence.
    Only an authoritative refusal supports a sampled no-listener claim. A
    connect reset (ECONNRESET) is a peer reset on an established/connecting
    path - an operational error, never absence - because a reset can be the
    proxy actively refusing a tunnel rather than proving no listener exists."""
    try:
        s = socket.create_connection(PROXY, timeout=0.4)
        s.close()
        return ("reachable", None)
    except OSError as exc:
        if exc.errno == socket.errno.ECONNREFUSED:
            return ("refused", None)
        return ("error", exc)

Reachable first probe is not failed — scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:226-239

Only an immediate refusal returns success; every other result is rechecked by sample_no_bind(), so a first successful connection can be forgotten if the second is refused.

def probe_refused_sampled(deadline, name, proc):
    """Post-signal no-listener witness: sample until the proxy port is
    authoritatively REFUSED. A connect that succeeds (admission stayed open) or
    an operational probe error both FAIL, so a broken observation boundary can
    never green the no-bind claim. Returns True once refused."""
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        kind, exc = connect_probe()
        if kind == "refused":
            return True
        if not sample_no_bind(name, proc):
            return False
        time.sleep(0.05)
    fail(name, "listener never observed authoritatively refused across the sampled post-signal interval (admission stayed open or observation gap)")
    return False

Fallback helper performs another connect — scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:168-190

sample_no_bind() discards prior observations and bases its result on a fresh TCP connection attempt.

def sample_no_bind(name, proc):
    """One interval-wide no-bind sample. A reachable connect or an operational
    probe error both FAIL with distinct details (reaping the binary); only an
    authoritative refusal is the expected no-listener state. Returns True when
    the sample observed refusal."""
    kind, exc = connect_probe()
    if kind == "reachable":
        proc.kill()
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=2)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            pass
        fail(name, "listener bound at a sampled probe point (interval-wide no-bind violated)")
        return False
    if kind == "error":
        proc.kill()
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=2)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            pass
        fail(name, f"operational connect error during no-bind sampling (indeterminate, not absence): {exc}")
        return False
    return True

Storm case relies on sampled no-admission witness — scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:1040-1048

The SIGTERM-storm case uses the flawed helper as its no-admission decision.

        t0 = time.monotonic()
        os.kill(proc.pid, signal.SIGTERM)
        # storm of repeat signals during the drain: none may move the deadline
        time.sleep(1.0)
        for _ in range(8):
            os.kill(proc.pid, signal.SIGTERM)
            time.sleep(0.05)
        if not probe_refused_sampled(t0 + 2.0, name, proc):
            return

Forced repeat case relies on same witness — scripts/e2e_shutdown.py:1199-1205

The repeat-SIGTERM case also accepts the helper's false-green decision.

        t0 = time.monotonic()
        os.kill(proc.pid, signal.SIGTERM)
        # no admissions after the first signal: the listener must be dropped
        # (error-aware sampling; an operational probe error never reads as
        # absence, so it fails the case rather than greening a broken probe)
        if not probe_refused_sampled(t0 + 2.0, name, proc):
            return

Validation

Confirmed the first probe classifies a successful connect as reachable, the helper does not fail it, and the fallback performs a second independent connect. Both named shutdown cases rely on this helper. The current proxy's shutdown correctness was not tested here. The assigned review independently confirms that reachable then refused can produce a false-green no-admission result in the forced and storm cases. The assigned worker independently traced the concrete first=reachable, second=refused, next=refused sequence through the harness pass outcome.

            proc.wait(timeout=2)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            pass
        fail(name, "listener bound at a sampled probe point (interval-wide no-bind violated)")
        return False
    if kind == "error":
        proc.kill()
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=2)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            pass
        fail(name, f"operational connect error during no-bind sampling (indeterminate, not absence): {exc}")
        return False
    return True

Reachability

Requires running the local E2E shutdown cases against a proxy implementation with delayed listener closure; no direct remote exploit of the current binary is established.

  • Attacker: Source-change contributor or faulty implementation being verified

  • Entry point: FORCED-REPEAT-NOADMIT and STORM-DURING-DRAIN E2E cases

  • Outcome: False-green no-admission verification

Severity

Low — This is a narrow security-verification false green during a timing race, not evidence that the current proxy admits post-shutdown clients. It affects local QA assurance and requires a listener that briefly remains open after SIGTERM; no deployed exposure or attacker control of SIGTERM was established.

A release process relying on these cases as its sole no-admission gate, or a source-backed ability for a workload to trigger this race, would raise severity; asserting failure on the first successful probe removes the gap.

Remediation

Fail immediately when the first connect_probe() returns reachable or error; retry only when no authoritative sample has yet been obtained, and never replace an observed success with a later refusal.

Tests:

  • Stub sequential probe results as reachable then refused and assert both shutdown cases fail.
  • Assert error then refused also fails rather than greening the no-admission witness.
  • Stub sequential probe results as reachable then refused and assert the helper fails.
  • Stub error then refused and assert failure; refused first should pass.

Preventive controls:

  • Make each sampled security invariant monotonic: once a violation is observed, later samples cannot turn the verdict green.
  • Keep probe classification and gate decision in one helper so every observed result is consumed exactly once.

Field Value

Affected lines src/runtime/reactor.rs:2989, src/runtime/reactor.rs:3002, src/runtime/reactor.rs:1382, src/runtime/tunnel.rs:563, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2939, src/runtime/reactor.rs:3039, src/runtime/reactor.rs:850, src/runtime/reactor.rs:2651, src/runtime/reactor.rs:837, src/runtime/reactor.rs:3342

Summary

A readiness batch can pass its expiry sweep, then cross an absolute deadline within a bounded serving visit. A late upstream connect can advance out of Dialing after its per-attempt deadline; a validated ClientHello write can open the forwarding gate after the ten-second setup deadline, call finish_setup, and clear that deadline; and a successful relay write can replace an expired idle deadline. Deadline expiry is checked at pre-dispatch and periodic batch boundaries but not at the protected connect acceptance, gate-opening write, setup graduation, or idle renewal. Those transitions can consume or replace an already expired deadline.

Validation

Static source tracing confirms three deadline transitions after a pre-dispatch or periodic sweep: late connect acceptance advances beyond Dialing, a ClientHello write can open the gate and graduate setup after the ten-second absolute deadline, and a relay write can renew an expired idle timer. In the setup case, finish_setup consumes the pending handle and the reactor clears setup_deadline, so the next sweep sees an established relay. No runtime timing test was executed.

Validation method: Independent static source validation

  • Status: validated

Counterevidence and remaining uncertainty:

  • The reactor sweeps deadlines before dispatch and periodically within a batch, limiting the timing window.
  • The client must pass exact allowlist, DNS peer, and ClientHello checks; no arbitrary egress results.
  • The connect attempt is clipped by the longer setup deadline; the bypass is of the per-attempt bound.

Dataflow

An authorized client drives a valid CONNECT, ClientHello, or established relay write near expiry, or an upstream TCP connection succeeds after its attempt deadline. A readiness batch passes its sweep while the deadline is live; later in the same serving visit, the post-expiry socket event or write advances the slot, opens the gate and forwards ClientHello bytes, or renews idle time without a fresh check.

Reachability

Time can elapse between the expiry sweep and each protected state transition. The attempt deadline is only applicable while Dialing; setup is graduated and its absolute deadline cleared; idle is replaced after a write. These state changes can hide the elapsed deadline from the next sweep.

Preconditions:

  • Client can reach the proxy and drive an otherwise valid allowed setup or established tunnel.
  • A gate-opening or relay write occurs after the corresponding deadline but within a visit that began before expiry.
  • For the connect facet, an upstream connection succeeds after its per-attempt deadline but before the next sweep while the setup deadline is still live.
  • Client can reach the proxy and send an otherwise valid allowlisted CONNECT and ClientHello.
  • The gate-opening write occurs across the ten-second setup deadline during a serving visit.

Existing controls:

  • Pre-dispatch and periodic batch expiry sweeps reduce the window but do not check the gate transition.

Severity

Low — A client needs narrow timing around an otherwise valid allowed setup or relay write, or a late upstream connection in a batch. The bypass can accept a tardy connect attempt, extend expired setup into relay, or preserve a tunnel past idle cutoff; destination and TLS identity checks still apply.

Additional runtime or deployment evidence could raise or lower this severity.

Remediation

Compare a fresh monotonic timestamp with the active connect, setup, and idle deadlines immediately before accepting a connect success, sending HTTP 200, writing any ClientHello bytes upstream, opening the forwarding gate, calling finish_setup, or renewing idle time. Reject or close an expired slot without forwarding further bytes; preserve the original absolute deadline until the guarded transition is valid. Test each connect, gate-opening and setup-graduation, and idle-renewal transition immediately before, at, and after expiry within one serving visit.

[21] Report-time detail loss can disappear from monitor summaries

Field Value
Severity low
Confidence high
Confidence rationale The summary-first ordering, drop increments, and unconditional dirty clear are direct source facts; a full-queue test confirms detail batch refusals. No runtime reproduction was performed.
Category Security telemetry integrity
CWE CWE-778
Affected lines src/log/mod.rs:986-1017, src/enforcement/monitor.rs:320-359, src/runtime/storage.rs:736-751, src/log/encoding.rs:834-842, src/runtime/storage.rs:736-751, src/enforcement/monitor.rs:346-364, src/log/encoding.rs:834-842, src/runtime/storage.rs:736-750, src/enforcement/monitor.rs:351-369, src/log/encoding.rs:827-843

Summary

A monitor report encodes and queues its summary before trying detail batches. If the log queue refuses a detail batch, the drop counter increments only after that summary was encoded. The storage caller then clears the monitor's dirty flag unconditionally. If no further monitor event occurs, the increased report_drops or capture_drops value is never emitted, even when the queued summary reaches the collector.

Root Cause

Report-time detail-drop accounting mutates Monitor after summary encoding, then mark_reported treats all resulting dirty state as already reported.

  • Attacker: client able to trigger monitored violations, combined with collector backpressure

  • Entry point: monitor report due during serving

  • Outcome: false zero or stale drop counter in delivered summary

Preconditions:

  • At least one monitor detail batch is pending.
  • The normal log queue is full when the batch is attempted.
  • No later monitor event triggers another summary.

Existing controls:

  • Reserved summary admission on a full queue.
  • Documentation warns counters may understate loss if a summary is itself lost.
  • Summary aggregate facts are retained in a reserved record when encoding succeeds.

Summary precedes detail batches — src/log/mod.rs:986-1002

The summary snapshots counters before a failed domain detail enqueue increments report_drops.

pub(crate) fn monitor_summary(&mut self, secs: u64, monitor: &mut Monitor) -> bool {
        self.set_now(secs);
        let committed = self.enqueue_reserved(Kind::Monitor, |buf| {
            let monitor_ref = &*monitor;
            encode_monitor_summary(buf, secs, monitor_ref)
        });
        if committed {
            let mut start = 0usize;
            let total = count_domain_batches(monitor);
            for part in 1..=total {
                let ok = self.enqueue_normal(|buf| {
                    let monitor_ref = &*monitor;
                    encode_monitor_domain_batch(buf, secs, part, total, monitor_ref, &mut start)
                });
                if !ok {
                    monitor.note_report_drop();
                }

Caller unconditionally marks reported — src/runtime/storage.rs:742-750

The caller does not preserve the dirty flag set during report-time detail loss.

{
            let monitor = self.enforcement.monitor_mut();
            self.logs.monitor_summary(secs, monitor);
        }
        if force {
            self.enforcement.mark_forced_monitor_reported();
        } else {
            self.enforcement.mark_monitor_reported(secs);
        }

Severity

Low — This can hide detail loss from the in-band counters operators use for alerting during stdout backpressure. It requires a full log queue and a detail-bearing monitor report, and later monitor activity can expose the cumulative counter.

Severity rises if operators use these counters as the sole loss signal during sustained adversarial traffic.

Impact assessment:

  • Level: low
  • Why: In-band loss alerting can miss dropped detail; cumulative counters remain in memory and can surface on later activity.

Likelihood assessment:

  • Level: medium
  • Why: Queue saturation requires sustained traffic and a slow collector.

Remediation

Preserve pending loss-report state when detail batches fail after summary encoding, then emit a follow-up reserved summary once capacity and cadence permit. Do not clear that pending state on normal or forced reporting; keep retry bounded. Alternatively, determine failed-detail counts before committing the summary.

Tests:

  • Fill the log queue, create domain and capture detail batches, report once, advance to the next second without new facts, and require a summary with the incremented drop counters.
  • Verify later activity still reports cumulative counters and no duplicate detail records are emitted.
  • Fill the log queue, trigger multiple domain and capture batches, and verify a later summary reports the resulting loss counters even when no new client event occurs.
  • Verify aggregate summary and detail accounting remain bounded under a stalled stdout sink.
  • Cover normal and forced monitor reporting with a full ring, then a quiet period, verifying the new report_drops and capture_drops values appear in a follow-up summary.

Preventive controls:

  • Keep report-time loss accounting in the same state transition that decides whether a summary remains due.
  • Make summary emission and post-summary detail-loss updates an explicit state machine so new loss cannot be erased by report completion.

A fixed prefix, process ID and sequential counter determine the shared-temp name.

fn temp_sink_file() -> std::fs::File {
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
    static COUNTER: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);

Field Value

Affected lines scripts/verify.sh:859-875, scripts/verify.sh:894-918, scripts/verify.sh:932-979, scripts/verify.sh:1813, src/lib.rs:8, scripts/verify.sh:890-917, scripts/verify.sh:1813

Summary

The offline docs verifier accepts a production .rs leaf symlink, but its preferred ripgrep unsafe scan does not follow that symlink. A contributor can point the leaf at a repository-controlled tests/*.rs target containing valid Rust with unsafe; the target path is allowlisted while the production module path is skipped. The assigned review also confirms a target with a non-.rs filename containing valid Rust: the source inventory admits the resolving link, while the scan omits both the link and the target extension. Either layout can print UNSAFE-SURFACE-OK for production-compiled unsafe code when the docs gate uses ripgrep.

Root Cause

The admitted source inventory and unsafe inspection disagree on symlink handling. A resolving production .rs leaf is admitted, but ripgrep does not traverse it; a tests/*.rs target is exempt by its target path, while a non-.rs target is omitted by the scan glob. The unsafe decision must be made for the production module path and its resolved content.

Ripgrep scan skips symlink targets — scripts/verify.sh:859-875

The preferred rg invocation lacks --follow; it classifies only returned paths and permits tests/*.

    if command -v rg >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        offenders="$(rg -l '\bunsafe\b' --glob '*.rs' --glob '!target/**' 2>/dev/null)" || scan_rc=$?
    else
        offenders="$(grep -Rl --include='*.rs' --exclude-dir=target --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=.ooda -E '\bunsafe\b' . 2>/dev/null)" || scan_rc=$?
        offenders=$(printf '%s\n' "$offenders" | sed 's#^\./##')
    fi

    done

intended_coverage_gate() {
    prc=0
    covered_rs="$(find src tests \( -type f -o -type l \) -name '*.rs' 2>&1)" || prc=$?

        echo "INTENDED-COVERAGE-FAIL: find exit $prc (tooling error, not PASS)" >&2
